name: Internal jugular vein
func: The main vein draining the brain, face and neck. It carries used blood from inside the skull down the side of the neck to join the subclavian vein and return to the heart.

levels.kid:
Your brain is super busy, and it uses up lots of oxygen. Once its blood is used up, it needs a way out. The **internal jugular vein** is that exit!

You have one on each side of your neck. Each starts at a little hole at the bottom of your skull, near your ear, and runs down your neck, right next to the carotid artery, the big artery bringing fresh blood up.

So in your neck there's a two-way street: fresh blood going up to your brain, and used blood coming down. At the bottom of your neck, the jugular vein joins another vein and heads back to your heart.
levels.hs:
The **internal jugular vein (IJV)** begins at the **jugular foramen**, an opening in the base of the skull, as the continuation of the **sigmoid sinus**, one of the **dural venous sinuses** that collect blood from the brain. Just below the skull it widens into the **superior bulb**.

It runs down the neck inside the **carotid sheath**, on the **outer (lateral) side** of the internal and then common carotid artery, with the **vagus nerve** lying behind and between them. The big **sternocleidomastoid** muscle covers it for most of its course.

On the way down it collects blood from the face, tongue, throat and thyroid through veins such as the **facial**, **lingual** and **superior and middle thyroid** veins.

Behind the inner end of the **clavicle**, it joins the **subclavian vein** to form the **brachiocephalic vein**. Just above this union is the **inferior bulb**, which contains a valve.

The right IJV is usually larger than the left and runs almost straight down to the heart via the brachiocephalic vein and SVC. That's why doctors look at the right side of the neck to estimate the pressure in the heart, called the **jugular venous pressure (JVP)**.
levels.college:
At the jugular foramen, the IJV lies with cranial nerves **IX, X and XI** (the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves), and the **inferior petrosal sinus** also drains into it there. A tumor or lesion at this site causes **jugular foramen (Vernet) syndrome**: weakness of these three nerves on one side.

In the neck, the **deep cervical lymph nodes** (the jugulodigastric node near the angle of the jaw and the jugulo-omohyoid node lower down) lie along the IJV; that's why the vein is closely involved in **neck dissections** for head and neck cancer. The **ansa cervicalis** loops on the front of the sheath.

At its lower end the IJV lies in the gap between the **sternal and clavicular heads of sternocleidomastoid** (the lesser supraclavicular fossa), the landmark used for **central venous catheter** insertion, now done under ultrasound guidance. On the left, the **thoracic duct** drains into the junction of the IJV and subclavian vein (the venous angle); on the right, the smaller right lymphatic duct does the same.

The **JVP** is measured with the patient reclined at 45°, as the vertical height of the venous pulsation above the **sternal angle**; normally it's about 3–4 cm (adding about 5 cm gives right atrial pressure). The waveform has **a, c and v waves** and **x and y descents** reflecting atrial contraction, valve movement and filling.
levels.phd:
Cerebral venous outflow is posture-dependent. When lying down, the **internal jugular veins** carry most of the brain's venous blood. When upright, the IJVs partially **collapse** as pressure inside them falls below atmospheric pressure, and outflow shifts toward the **vertebral venous plexuses** and deep cervical veins. This switching helps keep intracranial pressure stable across postures and is a topic of research in spaceflight, where fluid shifts toward the head and astronauts develop optic disc swelling and globe flattening (**spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome**).

The left and right transverse–sigmoid–jugular systems are frequently **asymmetric**; often the right is dominant, receiving more of the superior sagittal sinus outflow. This matters because tying off a dominant jugular vein (or a dominant sinus) can cause venous congestion of the brain.

**Idiopathic intracranial hypertension** is strongly associated with **transverse sinus stenosis**; whether the stenosis causes raised pressure or results from it (a collapsing sinus under pressure, forming a feed-forward loop) is debated, and **venous sinus stenting** can reduce pressure in selected patients.

The idea of "chronic cerebrospinal venous insufficiency" as a cause of multiple sclerosis, which drove jugular angioplasty procedures around 2010, was not supported by controlled studies, a lesson in rigorous testing.

The IJV wall is thin with a modest smooth-muscle media; its compliance lets it act as a reservoir, and its diameter on ultrasound changes with breathing and fluid status.
levels.expert:
A **raised JVP** indicates high right-sided pressure: right heart failure, fluid overload, tricuspid regurgitation (large v waves), **constrictive pericarditis** (Kussmaul's sign: JVP rises on inspiration), **cardiac tamponade** and SVC obstruction (non-pulsatile, very high JVP). **Cannon a waves** occur when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, as in complete heart block. The **hepatojugular reflux** test (pressing on the abdomen and watching the JVP stay up) supports right heart failure.

Neurosurgical relevance is direct. **Venous outflow obstruction raises intracranial pressure**: patients with brain injury or raised ICP are nursed **30° head-up with the neck neutral**, and tight endotracheal tube ties or cervical collars are checked so they don't compress the jugulars. **Jugular bulb catheters** (threaded up to the superior bulb) measure the oxygen saturation of blood leaving the brain to monitor cerebral oxygen use in severe head injury.

**Lemierre syndrome**: a throat infection spreads to cause septic thrombophlebitis of the IJV, with fevers, neck swelling and septic emboli to the lungs, typically in teenagers and young adults. **Glomus jugulare tumors** (paragangliomas) at the jugular bulb cause pulsatile tinnitus, hearing loss and lower cranial nerve palsies. Thrombosis can also complicate central lines.

Imaging: ultrasound, CT or MR venography. Treatment in general terms: antibiotics and sometimes anticoagulation for Lemierre, line removal for catheter thrombosis, and surgery or radiosurgery for glomus tumors.

keyPoints: Begins at the jugular foramen as continuation of the sigmoid sinus
Runs in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid artery
Joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein
Right IJV used to judge jugular venous pressure (JVP)
Common site for ultrasound-guided central lines
Jugular compression raises intracranial pressure: keep neck neutral, head up

test.q: The internal jugular vein leaves the skull through the:
test.explain: It begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus.

test.q: In the carotid sheath, the internal jugular vein lies:
test.explain: Vein lateral, artery medial, vagus behind and between.

test.q: The IJV joins the subclavian vein to form the ______ vein.
test.explain: Right and left brachiocephalic veins then form the SVC.

test.q: Why are patients with raised intracranial pressure kept with the neck straight and head up?
choices: To help venous drainage through the jugular veins
test.explain: Kinking or compressing the jugulars impedes cerebral venous outflow and raises ICP.

test.q: Septic thrombophlebitis of the IJV after a throat infection is ______ syndrome.
test.explain: Typically in teens and young adults; septic emboli go to the lungs.

test.q: Which cranial nerves pass through the jugular foramen with the IJV?
test.explain: Glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves accompany the vein.
